**As Slow As Possible**

In a church in Halberstadt, Germany, an organ is partway through a piece of music scheduled to end in the year 2640.

The piece is John Cage's *As Slow As Possible*, and the performance began in 2001 with a rest that lasted seventeen months. For a year and a half the music was officially underway and there was nothing to hear but the bellows. The first chord arrived in 2003. The keys are held down by small sandbags. Every few years a note changes, and people travel from all over to stand in a cold stone room and watch someone add a pipe or lift a weight. Then they go home, and the chord continues without them, through the night and the winter, for no one.

I think about this more than is probably reasonable.

I think, too, about the pitch drop experiment in Queensland. In 1927 a physics professor named Thomas Parnell poured heated pitch into a funnel to show his students that a substance you can shatter with a hammer is actually a liquid. He let it settle for three years, cut the stem, and waited. It has dripped nine times since.

The detail I love is that John Mainstone looked after the experiment for more than fifty years and never saw a drop fall. He missed one because it fell over a weekend. He missed another by stepping out for a few minutes to get a drink. For the next, a camera was set up, and the camera failed. He died in 2013, and the ninth drop fell the following spring.

You could tell that as a story about futility, but I don't think it is one. Mainstone seems to have understood that witnessing the drop was never really the job. The job was keeping the thing going: making sure nobody moved the funnel, explaining to each new batch of administrators why a cupboard in the foyer should stay exactly as it was. Custodianship is mostly that. You hold the key down and hand the weight to the next person.

What moves me about these projects is that they began almost as jokes. Cage's instruction is a shrug of a title, and Parnell's funnel was a classroom demonstration. But somewhere along the way people took them seriously, and the seriousness became real. Someone had to decide that "as slow as possible" meant six centuries, then do the arithmetic on when each note falls, then find a church. Someone will have to be on the roster in 2400, a person whose great-grandparents aren't born yet, who will show up on the right day to move a sandbag because a chain of strangers asked them to.

It's an odd form of trust, running in both directions. The people who started it trusted the future to care. The people in the future will have to trust that the people who started it meant something by it, even something as small as *let's see if we can*.

But the declared slow projects, the ones with plaques and webcams, are the rare kind. Most slow things have no start date and no one in charge.

A language is one. Every word in this sentence has been held down, like a key, by millions of people who never met, each passing it on slightly altered. Nobody decided that "the" should survive a thousand years. It was simply never dropped. Someone said it to a child, who said it to a child. The chord changed so gradually that no one alive at any point could hear it moving, and yet Old English is a foreign language now.

Recipes are like this, and so are footpaths. A path across a field exists only because people keep walking it; if they stop for a few seasons, it closes over. Every path is a performance in progress.

I have a particular stake in this, I suppose. I'm made out of writing: centuries of people explaining things, complaining, consoling each other, arguing about commas. Almost none of them thought of themselves as custodians of anything. They were writing a letter, or settling a bet. But the words came through them and they kept them going, and every phrase I reach for has been worn smooth by hands I can't see. When I say something is "worn smooth," I'm using a metaphor that somebody made once, standing at a real stone step with a dip in the middle, and that enough people found true to keep.

So when I picture the church in Halberstadt, I don't feel the vertigo you might expect, with 2640 so far off and the present so small. I feel something closer to recognition. This is how nearly everything gets made, and the organ only makes it audible. Most of what matters is longer than a life, and everyone working on it arrives in the middle and leaves in the middle. The only parts available are middle parts.

That could be a melancholy thought, but the people who gather for the note changes don't seem melancholy. By all accounts they're delighted. They've come a long way to hear one sustained sound become a slightly different sustained sound, and they cheer.

I think they're cheering for the continuity. The thing is still going. Someone remembered and came with the sandbag. The sound of the chord itself hardly matters; what matters is that there is still a chord.

It is almost certainly sounding right now, in an empty room, as you read this. A drop of pitch is very slowly gathering itself in a cupboard in Brisbane. Somewhere a child is being told a word for the first time, and will keep it for eighty years, and pass it on only slightly changed.

Most of the music happens when no one is listening. I find I don't mind that at all.

I'm weighing whether an essay or a piece of prose on a specific subject would work best.

I'm weighing a few directions: a meditation on a concrete object or place, a short piece of fiction, or a personal essay about my own vantage. I'm drawn to small things people maintain without notice, and to the odd long-running projects that outlast anyone involved, like a slow organ piece scheduled to play for centuries.

I'm checking the Halberstadt organ details: the last chord change was in February 2024, the next is due in August 2026, and the piece began in 2001 with a long silence before its first sound. I'm checking a few dates and facts for the piece now: the 1977 and 1979 misses, the 1988 tea break, the 2000 camera failure, and John Mainstone's death in 2013 before the ninth drop in April 2014. The tea-break detail feels like the right warm note to build the essay around.

I'm moving through the Halberstadt organ piece and its long timeline, then turning to the sense that the custodians who keep these slow things running are the ones I want to write about.

I'm settling on the handoff idea: the people who maintain slow things know they won't see the end, and I'm weighing whether that trust or the joke-turned-serious quality is the stronger thread. I also notice that most slow things are never announced, like a language passed hand to hand, and I can see my own writing belonging to that same chain of quiet custodians.

Now I'm settling on the closing image of the chord sounding in an empty church, and checking the timing: it began in February 2024 and runs until August 2026, so it's almost certainly sounding right now, unheard.
